metadata.title: Improving Alignment Between Human and Machine Codes: An Empirical Assessment of Prompt Engineering for Construct Identification in Psychology

abstract: Due to their architecture and vast pre-training data, large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong text classification performance. However, LLM output - here, the category assigned to a text - depends heavily on the wording of the prompt. While literature on prompt engineering is expanding, few studies focus on classification tasks, and even fewer address domains like psychology, where constructs have precise, theory-driven definitions that may not be well represented in pre-training data. We present an empirical framework for optimizing LLM performance for identifying constructs in texts via prompt engineering. We experimentally evaluate five prompting strategies --codebook-guided empirical prompt selection, automatic prompt engineering, persona prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, and explanatory prompting - with zero-shot and few-shot classification. We find that persona, chain-of-thought, and explanations do not fully address performance loss accompanying a badly worded prompt. Instead, the most influential features of a prompt are the construct definition, task framing, and, to a lesser extent, the examples provided. Across three constructs and two models, the classifications most aligned with expert judgments resulted from a few-shot prompt combining codebook-guided empirical prompt selection with automatic prompt engineering. Based on our findings, we recommend that researchers generate and evaluate as many prompt variants as feasible, whether human-crafted, automatically generated, or ideally both, and select prompts and examples based on empirical performance in a training dataset, validating the final approach in a holdout set. This procedure offers a practical, systematic, and theory-driven method for optimizing LLM prompts in settings where alignment with expert judgment is critical.

Improving Alignment Between Human and Machine Codes:
An Empirical Assessment of Prompt Engineering for Construct
Identification in Psychology

Abstract
Due to their architecture and vast pre-training data, large language models (LLMs)
demonstrate strong text classification performance.
However, LLM output—here,
the category assigned to a text—depends heavily on the wording of the prompt.
While literature on prompt engineering is expanding, few studies focus on classifi-
cation tasks, and even fewer address domains like psychology, where constructs have
precise, theory-driven definitions that may not be well represented in pre-training data.
We present an empirical framework for optimizing LLM performance for identifying
constructs in texts via prompt engineering. We experimentally evaluate five prompting
strategies—codebook-guided empirical prompt selection, automatic prompt engineer-
ing, persona prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, and explanatory prompting—with
zero-shot and few-shot classification. We find that persona, chain-of-thought, and ex-
planations do not fully address performance loss accompanying a badly worded prompt.
Instead, the most influential features of a prompt are the construct definition, task
framing, and, to a lesser extent, the examples provided. Across three constructs and
two models, the classifications most aligned with expert judgments resulted from a
few-shot prompt combining codebook-guided empirical prompt selection with auto-
matic prompt engineering.
Based on our findings, we recommend that researchers
generate and evaluate as many prompt variants as feasible—whether human-crafted,
automatically generated, or ideally both—and select prompts and examples based on
empirical performance in a training dataset, validating the final approach in a hold-
out set. This procedure offers a practical, systematic, and theory-drive method for
optimizing LLM prompts in settings where alignment with expert judgment is critical.

Introduction
Psychology is largely the study of internal processes—of thoughts, feelings, and mental
states that occur within the mind. As such, psychological constructs of interest, such as
specific emotions or thought patterns, are often latent and cannot be directly observed. In
clinical and research settings, however, these constructs may be inferred from what a client
says, in writing or in speech (Stavropoulos, Crone, and Grossmann 2024). For example,
the client may reveal negative core beliefs (overgeneralized judgments about themselves,
others, or the world; Beck 2011; Wenzel 2012) during a therapy session. Alternatively, they
may demonstrate positive meaning making (identifying positive change or growth due to a
negative experience; Boals 2012) when writing about a difficult experience. Measuring these
and other latent constructs – whether to assess outcomes, identify mediators, or develop
theory – often involves the labeling of text data.
Commonly it is experts who generate such labeled data by combing through and classi-
fying text segments. This process of hand-coding comes with substantial challenges, partic-
ularly as the size of the data scales, including: costs, delays, coder fatigue, and coder drift
(Can et al. 2016). Alternatively, researchers may train a supervised learning algorithm to
replicate the labeling process of human experts by leveraging statistical patterns learned in
the hand-labeled dataset to classify new unlabeled text segments automatically (Dehghani
et al. 2017; Semeraro et al. 2023; Shin, Pinto, and Wang 2025). This approach is imminently
scalable – the cost of classifying an additional text segment after model training is negli-
gible – but its effectiveness depends heavily on the quantity of labeled training data, with
quantities in the thousands commonly required.
Recent developments in natural language processing bring a new option: automatic text
classification using large language models (LLMs). In this approach, researchers use general-
purpose pre-trained LLMs to classify unlabeled text segments according to the constructs of
interest (e.g., Martinez 2024; Genugten and Schacter 2024). Pre-trained LLMs begin a new
task with a substantial advantage compared to their traditionally supervised counterparts.
From their enormous general purpose training datasets, they have already learned linguistic
patterns capturing diverse word meanings, grammatical structures, and idiomatic patterns.
Thus, the pre-training process underlying LLMs dramatically lowers the necessary number
of labeled examples required to reach a high level of model accuracy. Indeed, in what is
called zero-shot classification a researcher simply prompts the LLM to categorize a segment
of text using natural language instructions without any context-specific training data at all
(Reynolds and McDonell 2021). However, performance is often variable and highly dependent
on the specific wording within the prompt provided to the LLM (W. Chen, Koenig, and
Dilkina 2024). Thus, prompt engineering, a systematic and iterative process of optimizing
prompt design to improve LLM performance on specific tasks, has emerged as a feasible and
impactful lever for improving the alignment between human and machine codes.
In the technical literature, prompt engineering is approached as an empirical method,
often involving structured comparisons across prompt variations and evaluation against per-
formance metrics. When treated this way, there is substantial evidence that prompt engi-
neering can improve the quality of LLM output (Kojima et al. 2022; Weber and Reichardt
2023; Zhou et al. 2022). However, the prompt engineering literature remains limited for psy-
chological and behavioral researchers in at least a few key areas. First, the majority of the
prompt engineering literature focuses on text generation (e.g., asking a model to answer an
open-ended question) rather than text classification (where the model should select between
a limited number of options in its response), leaving prompt engineering methods for text
classification underdeveloped (White et al. 2023). This is particularly problematic given re-
search has demonstrated that LLM performance on close-ended questions, like classification
tasks, is “remarkably unremarkable” compared to its text generation capabilities (Reynolds
and McDonell 2021, p. 5). Second, many commonly recommended prompt engineering ap-
proaches, like chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022) are not straightforward to apply
to text classification scenarios as they encourage long and variable responses from a model
and have less evidence of efficacy within the classification context (Lampinen et al. 2022).
Finally, there is very little research testing the efficacy of prompt engineering techniques in
psychological and behavioral sciences. Thus, it is often unclear how prompt engineering ap-
proaches will perform on complex, field-specific tasks (Stavropoulos, Crone, and Grossmann
2024) where understandings of terms may differ from the largely non-academic documents
on which the LLMs were trained (Ziems et al. 2024).
2

This article fills that gap by conducting a series of prompt engineering case studies, sys-
tematically testing over a thousand varied prompts for identifying psychological constructs
across variable contexts. While in practice, prompting is often treated as an ad hoc and
qualitative process, in this paper, we treat it as a computational problem, leveraging pro-
grammatic experimentation to test prompt effectiveness across diverse tasks, models, and
samples. In doing so, we demonstrate how these methods and techniques may be rigorously
applied and use the results to draw out recommendations for future researchers. Our case
studies focus on three text classification tasks, one which we view as a low-inference task
that closely matches a common general-use purpose of text classifiers (emotion identifica-
tion), and two higher-inference tasks with precise, theory-driven definitions: identifying 1)
negative core beliefs and 2) positive meaning making in participant writing samples. This
combination of tasks was chosen to evaluate how well commonly recommended prompting
methods work with different levels of task difficulty and field specificity.
In our experiments, we distinguish between what we term baseline prompts and additive
techniques. Baseline prompts are defined here as prompts that simply describe the construct
and the classification task. Additive techniques are additional modifications that can be
layered onto any baseline prompt, regardless of the construct being classified. In total, we
evaluate two approaches to generating baseline prompts (human-generated/codebook-guided
empirical prompt selection and automatic prompt engineering), three additive prompting
techniques (persona pattern, chain-of-thought, and explanations), and two uses of labeled
examples (zero-shot and few-shot), on three constructs (gratitude, negative core beliefs, and
positive meaning making), and four samples (online message board posts from 590 Reddit
users, clinical writing samples from 160 young adults with a mental health diagnosis, from
175 mothers with a mental health diagnosis, and from 68 women who recently experienced
sexual assault). Each combination involves multiple prompt variants, with some techniques
tested using dozens or even hundreds of prompt iterations, resulting in thousands of total
evaluations.
The breadth and scale in our experiments allow us to 1) assess state-of-the-art prompt
engineering methods; 2) demonstrate a comprehensive LLM text classification process; 3)
test the robustness of these recommendations to variation in tasks and data, and 4) pro-
vide recommendations to the field. Across constructs and models, we find that it is the
baseline prompt – whether human engineered or automatically engineered – which is most
determinative of alignment with human codes. Our human-generated prompts often out-
perform the automatically engineered prompt but not to such an extent we would dismiss
the value of automatic prompt engineering. Indeed, our best performing prompts were most
often prompts that were generated first by identifying the best-performing human-generated
prompt, then incorporating automatic prompt engineering. Adding few-shot examples also
reliably produced small improvements. On the other hand, the additive techniques tested
(personas, chain-of-thought, and explanations) offered only marginal improvements at best.
Further, improvements with additive techniques were only observed when added to low per-
forming baseline prompts, again emphasizing that it is the construct definition and task
description which matters most for improving model performance. Unfortunately, however,
identifying the best prompt cannot be done a priori but can only be determined by testing
multiple prompts in a labeled dataset that is large enough to produce credible performance
estimates. In our case, doing so improved model performance on a relatively low-inference
construct by as much as 16% and on a high-inference construct by as much as 75%; mean-
ingful improvements which ultimately increase the validity of the LLM-based measures when
employed.
Background
A Brief Introduction to LLMs and Prompting
Generative LLMs are designed to generate text continuations.
Given text provided
by a user – the prompt – they generate reasonable subsequent words by identifying high-
probability continuations that reproduce patterns observed in their training data (Hussain
et al. 2024). Within the text classification context, for example, the LLM might identify a
high probability next word for the following prompt:
“Negative core beliefs are generalized or exaggerated judgments people have

about themselves, others, or the world. Does the following text contain an ex-
ample of the psychological concept of a negative core belief? Respond Yes or
No.”

Depending on the content of the text, the next most likely word will be either “Yes” or “No.”

Where D is a document (e.g., user-provided text followed by model-generated text) consisting
of tokens (i.e., words, word fragments, and common phrases; Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch
2015) i through n such that D = {u1, u2, ...un} (Alec Radford et al. 2018). The objective
function of D (which is maximized) is the aggregate of the (log) probabilities of each token,

The conditional
probability of each next token is modeled using a transformer model (large neural networks
with multi-head attention mechanisms) with parameters θ estimated in the pre-training data
(Alec Radford et al. 2018, A. Radford et al. 2019; Vaswani et al. 2017). In summary, and
put more simply, the model aims to maximize the probability of a next token, conditional
on the previous tokens in a document. Thus, a key mechanism for determining LLM output
is to adjust these previous tokens – the prompt.
Baseline Prompting
Formally, prompting can be understood as a form of conditioning; more practically, the
prompt sets the context for the desired response, telling the LLM what information to pay
attention to, and designating the desired output content and format (White et al. 2023).
Together, we refer to these components as a baseline prompt.
Given a baseline prompt
is written in natural language (as opposed to artificial language or computer code), often a
reasonable starting place is the same set of instructions which would be provided to a human
(Gilardi, Alizadeh, and Kubli 2023; Michelmann et al. 2025). For example, in Prompt A
above, we provided the context (defining negative core beliefs), and designate both the
desired output (e.g., tasking the LLM with determining if negative core beliefs are evidence
in some text) and format (“Yes” or “No”).
Intuition and theory suggest that baseline prompts are most effective when instructions
are unambiguous and specific (B. Chen et al. 2023; Lo 2023). Other practical (though not
always empirical) advice includes ensuring that the label provided for the text classification
task (here, negative core beliefs) match common usage of language so the LLM can locate
the definition of the construct within the pretraining data (Gao, Fisch, and D. Chen 2020).
Additional guidance suggests incorporating bullet points to increase clarity (Mishra et al.
2021) and preferencing positive rather than negative statements (Battle and Gollapudi 2024).
Other suggestions remain contested. For example, while Reynolds and McDonell 2021 argue
that redundancy in prompting can enhance performance, Mishra et al. 2021 recommend
prioritizing conciseness to avoid confusion or overload.
Unfortunately, the best performing baseline prompt is not always intuitive (Battle and
Gollapudi 2024). Indeed, the best performing prompt may not even be sensical to human
readers (Battle and Gollapudi 2024). This is one reason why automatic prompt engineer-
ing can be a useful approach. Automatic prompt engineering supplements hand-designed
prompts by 1) using the LLM to iteratively generate a set of alternative prompts given a
seed prompt, 2) selecting the highest performing prompt among the alternatives and using
this as the next seed (Zhou et al. 2022). Previous tests of this approach have indicated mixed
performance, with the automatically engineered prompt sometimes performing worse than
the default but often performing comparable or better (Zhou et al. 2022). Notably, when
automatic prompt engineering works, it is not because the LLM has a strong understanding
of how different prompts will work on itself (W. Chen, Koenig, and Dilkina 2024) but simply
because of brute force. “Seemingly worthless prompt modifications” can have meaningful
performance impacts (Battle and Gollapudi 2024, p. 1).
4

The Use of Examples
Eliciting accurate classifications from an LLM without examples or demonstrations –
i.e. via zero-shot classification – can be difficult. As an alternative, one-shot classification
not only provides a task but also a demonstration of it (Brown et al. 2020; Weber and
Reichardt 2023). For example, to use one-shot, we would extend upon Prompt A, with one
example of a written response from a participant that has been labeled with either “Yes”
or “No” (indicating a negative core belief, or not). In doing so, we provide the model with
a clear demonstration of the task at hand. Few-shot classification extends the principle of
one-shot classification by increasing the number of examples and thus providing additional
context-specific knowledge on the task (Brown et al. 2020). The number of demonstrations
in few-shot learning is up to the user and can range between as few as two and as many as
dozens (Brown et al. 2020).
Additive Prompting Techniques
Recent research into prompt engineering has often focused on what we term here additive
prompt engineering techniques. These include broadly applicable techniques that may be
applied to any baseline prompt. In what follows, we examine three prompting techniques,
ordered by the degree of adaptation they require—from minimal to substantial.
Persona Pattern
A persona pattern is a short phrase, commonly added to the beginning of the prompt,
which provides the LLM with either a role to play or a characteristic to embody (White et al.
2023). For example, we might append, “You are a therapist” or “You are a psychologist”
ahead of our task descriptions. The key motivation underlying a persona pattern is the idea
that the researcher may not know what details of the task need to be specified in the prompt
but will likely know the types of people who could successfully complete the task (White
et al. 2023). In theory, appending a persona patterns works because it draws on a kind of
“cultural consciousness” associated with the role (Reynolds and McDonell 2021, p. 4). In
calling on the therapist or psychologist role, for example, we hope that the model is also
activating patterns associated with negative core beliefs in the psychology context. To our
knowledge, evidence underlying the effectiveness of the persona pattern is largely anecdotal
rather than experimental. However, Battle and Gollapudi 2024 have conducted a series of
experiments on the efficacy of a related approach – termed positive thinking. A positive
thinking prompt simply appends an upbeat phrase to the task. Often, this is combined
with a role – as in “You are an expert mathematician” but may simply be a characteristic,
as in “You are highly intelligent” (Battle and Gollapudi 2024, p. 2). While a theory has
not been outlined for why positive thinking without a role would be useful, the authors
conclude that, in most – but not all - instances, the prompt addition positively impacted
model performance.
Chain-of-Thought Prompting
Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought. Zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting involves adding
a simple phrase such as, “Let’s think this through step by step” to the end of a prompt (Ko-
jima et al. 2022). Despite the simplicity of the approach, the addition of this phrase has
significantly improved LLM performance on a range of benchmark tasks including arithmetic
and symbolic reasoning (Kojima et al. 2022), perhaps because it encourages the decomposi-
tion of problems into smaller more simple subtasks.
In a text classification context, chain-of-thought prompting requires minor adaptation.
The chain-of-thought prompt purposefully elicits long-winded answers from the model – the
multistep reasoning (Kojima et al. 2022). However, in text classification tasks, only one of
a few answer choices are accepted. One approach is to request the model to provide its
reasoning, and then to provide a final answer in a specified format. For example, we might
provide adapted instructions such as: “First, explain your reasoning step by step. Then,
state your final answer — either Yes or No — using the format: Final Answer: [Yes or No].”
Few-Shot Chain-of-Thought Prompting. Few-shot chain-of-thought prompting is
the predecessor to the zero-shot chain-of-thought approach described above. In few-shot
5

chain-of-thought prompting, reasoning is not just encouraged (via a phrase) but demon-
strated with examples (Wei et al. 2022). In addition to providing input-output pairs as
exemplars, few-shot chain-of-thought prompting includes intermediate natural language rea-
soning steps that lead to the final answer (Wei et al. 2022). Here is one potential example
of a reasoning example we could provide, within the context of identifying positive meaning
making and paired with a participant writing about their mother’s death: “First, I see that
the excerpt is indeed about a negative event (here, a mother’s death). Second, I see that the
writer identifies a positive outcome (they’ve become stronger). Third, I see that the writer
attributes the positive outcome to the negative event. Because of these three points, my final
answer is yes. Final Answer: Yes.” This kind of few-shot approach simultaneously demon-
strates how the task should be completed, identifies what in the participant text needs to be
attended to, and exemplifies how the response should be formatted. As with zero-shot chain-
of-thought prompting, few-shot chain-of-thought prompting has a substantial evidence base
underlying it (Wei et al. 2022). However, there are cases where few-shot chain-of-thought
has had adverse effects on model performance (Anil et al. 2023; Battle and Gollapudi 2024).
Explanations
Explanations are justifications provided with few-shot examples (Lampinen et al. 2022).
The key difference between the above approach (few-shot chain-of-thought prompting) and
explanations is the order: with chain-of-thought, the justification occurs before the answer
choice. With explanations, the justification is provided after. Perhaps surprisingly, this can
make a difference. While the former is designed to elicit multi-step thinking, the latter is
designed to highlight task principles that allow the model to generalize broadly (Lampinen
et al. 2022). Further, these two approaches likely differ in the weight provided to the jus-
tification compared to the exemplar answers. Due to recency bias, whichever occurs last
is likely to be given the greater weight by the model (Liu et al. 2023). Thus, explanation
prompting likely weights the justification more heavily than the example-answer pair. The
typical structure of an explanation few-shot prompt (here, for text classification) is to provide
the task instruction, the example text, the classification of the example, and an explana-
tion of the response (Lampinen et al. 2022). When the LLM provides its own response, the
LLMs explanation can either be ignored or observed to gain intuition into information the
model is drawing upon. Lampinen et al. 2022 find that the explanation prompt can improve
performance on a wide variety of tasks (Lampinen et al. 2022).
Contribution
Unfortunately, prior research indicates that none of the above can be counted on to
reliably improve performance. For example, while chain-of-thought prompting has at times
demonstrated significant improvements in model performance (Wei et al. 2022), in other
studies, it has demonstrated an adverse effect (Anil et al. 2023). Further, model performance
can depend on seemingly minute changes in prompt wording, exemplar selection, and even
exemplar order (Sahoo et al. 2024; Zhao et al. 2021). Here we address the seemingly erratic
nature of prompting with LLMs by first, searching for generalizable patterns across three
constructs and two models, and second, by formulating a reasonable prompt engineering
protocol which can be used across diverse text classification tasks.
Case Study Experiments and Data
LLMs tend to be reliable text classifiers for low-inference concepts like sentiment or
discrete emotions (Rathje et al. 2024). However, high-inference concepts that have a complex,
field-specific meaning – what Ziems et al. 2024 refer to as expert taxonomies, terms which
are either uncommon, or do not match the meaning the in the pre-training corpora – pose a
more difficult challenge. Here, we design our experiments to capture a spectrum of scenarios
from low complexity to high complexity, both with and without, expert taxonomies.

Low Complexity – Emotion Identification
We generate a low-inference task by drawing on a dataset created by Demszky et al.
2020 of Reddit posts labelled with the emotions they express. The original dataset includes
over 58,000 Reddit posts, labelled with 26 emotions by 3-5 labelers each (described as native
English speakers from India). Inter-rater reliability in that dataset ranges from a Cohen’s
Kappa of 0.144 (for nervousness) to 0.749 (for gratitude). For the purposes of this study,
we focus on the emotion with the highest inter-rater reliability – gratitude – as this high
reliability suggests a low-complexity task. We also limit our analysis to a random sample of
600 texts (a size which is more reflective of psychological studies), 300 of which were labelled
as expressing gratitude (defined by Demszky et al. 2020 as “a feeling of thankfulness and
appreciation,” pg. 12).
Higher Complexity – Negative Core Beliefs and Positive Meaning
Making
The above case study introduces a relatively low-inference task on which non-expert hu-
man labelers were able to reach high reliability. However, many constructs in psychology
are complex (with definitions including multiple components), high-inference (necessitating
interpretation) and require some level of specialized knowledge. To assess the usefulness of
common prompt-engineering techniques in these more challenging scenarios, we experiment
with two additional constructs: negative core beliefs and positive meaning making. We define
negative core beliefs as broad, generalized, or exaggerated negative judgments people have
about themselves, others, or the world (Beck 2011). We define positive meaning making as
occurring when a person reports some positive change or outcome resulting from a negative
event, trauma, or stressor in their life (Boals 2012). We identify instances of negative core
beliefs and positive meaning making from text produced within expressive writing interven-
tions (Reinhold, B¨urkner, and Holling 2018), where the participants engaged in independent,
reflective writing over a brief period.
Here, we draw from three current or recently completed studies of expressive writing,
including in a sample of young (ages 21 to 30) biological or trans- women who have been
previously diagnosed with a mental health condition, a sample of mothers with a mental
health history, and a sample of college women who had experienced sexual assault within
the past year. Taken together, our sample includes 437 unique individuals responding to
between one and three expressive writing tasks; 565 texts were labelled for negative core
beliefs and 589 texts were labeled for meaning making. Both were labelled by a combination
of trained undergraduate students and psychology graduate students.
Table 1 provides
information on the distribution of construct prevalence and inter-rater reliability. Inter-rater
reliability (Cohen’s Kappa; Cohen 1960) was estimated to be 0.82 for negative core beliefs
and 0.70 for meaning making. (While we would hypothesize that, of the three constructs,
Cohen’s Kappa would be highest for gratitude, in practice, it is highest for negative core

as a more complex construct than gratitude and attribute the higher Cohen’s Kappa as due
to our coder background, training, and consensus-building process.)
Strengths and Limitations of the Case Studies
Our case studies offer three key strengths. First, they span a range of task complexity,
from low-inference classification (e.g., emotion recognition) to higher-inference construct

assess the usefulness of prompting techniques under differing levels of challenge. Second,
the latter two concepts (negative core beliefs and meaning making) represent constructs
that require LLMs to use “unique reasoning paths not typically encountered. . . during their
pre-training phase” (Lee et al. 2024). Presumably, prompt engineering is of even greater
importance for such constructs. Third, the writing which is classified reflects writing collected
in the real-world, including spelling errors, irrelevant content, and texts for which two experts
can reasonably disagree. On the other hand, our data still contain generalizability challenges.
Notably, all the data collected for negative core beliefs and meaning making was generated
by women. This would be of particular concern if our goal was to assess the performance of
LLMs or to suggest the best prompt for these constructs. Instead, our goal is to assess the
usefulness of prompt engineering approaches. Thus, the limited diversity of our sample will
only threaten our results if there is a reason to believe, for example, that persona prompts
work better or worse for women’s writing compared to men. Second, it is possible that
the data drawn from Reddit may have been included in the training of the LLMs we are
using. Thus, there are two potential reasons we might expect the LLM to exhibit higher
performance on gratitude than on our expressive writing tasks: the expressive writing tasks
involve a higher level of complexity and the text contained in the Reddit data may very well
have been encountered in the training of the LLMs used, i.e., GPT and/or Llama, creating
leakage and the possible overinflation of performance metrics (Kaufman et al. 2012). The
expressive writing samples, on the other hand, have not been publicly released so they were
certainly not.
Methods
We began by splitting our data at the participant level into training, development, and
testing datasets. The training dataset was used to pilot prompts and to provide examples
for few-shot learning. The development dataset was used to compare the performance of the
additive prompting techniques after finalizing wording in the training dataset. We held our
testing dataset until the final prompt and model for each concept was selected. Thus, this
dataset provides a best estimate of the final performance of the LLM for each construct.
We split our data such that 25% of individuals are placed in the training dataset, 50% into
the development dataset, and 25% into the testing dataset. We chose this distribution for two
reasons. First, compared to training a supervised learning classifier from scratch, our training
needs are limited. Thus, more resources can be distributed to comparing approaches and
validating the final model. Second, given the key purpose of this manuscript is to compare
prompting approaches in order to provide recommendations to future researchers, we devote
the majority of our labeled data to this purpose. Still, as a demonstration of best practice,
we retain a testing dataset which was unseen during any portion of the model development
process to assess the performance of the final selected model.
Table 2 provides sample sizes for each of our constructs and data splits (training, devel-
opment, and testing). Because these are secondary data, we did not conduct priori power
analyses. However, we made use of all relevant clinical text data available to us and allo-
cated participants so as to maximize statistical precision in the comparison of prompting
approaches while still retaining a test set for final evaluation.
Further, by keeping our
training, testing, and validation datasets independent, we limit the threat of over-inflated
performance metrics (Anglin 2024).
When assessing the performance of our prompts, we use four criteria: accuracy, preci-
sion, recall, and F1. Each of these depends on the relationship between true positives (i.e.,
8

instances where the LLM correctly identifies an instance of the construct), false positives
(incorrectly identifying the construct), false negatives (incorrectly identifying the absence
of the construct), and true negatives (correctly identifying the absence of the construct).
Here, the determination of “true” and “false” depends on alignment with the human label.
(Though the use of these terms is something of a shorthand, given we know that human
labels bring their own error, a fact exemplified by our assessment of inter-rater reliability).

Baseline Prompts and Examples
Codebook-Guided Human-Generated Prompts
In line with best practices for codebook development, our baseline prompts incorporate
three components: a brief definition of the target construct (e.g., negative core beliefs),
a task instruction (e.g., “classify the following text. . . ”), and potential inclusion/exclusion
criteria (MacQueen et al. 1998). We hypothesize that each of these elements may influence
LLM performance. To test this, we created five variants each of the construct definition
and the task instruction. All variants were generated manually without referencing to prior
writing, in order to encourage linguistic diversity.
(We also intentionally avoided LLM-
generated variants here, as automated prompts are built into automated prompt engineering
process discussed later.) From our human-generated codebook, we also identified n potential
inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Then, using the following procedure, we generated 50 prompt variants:
1. Randomly select one construct definition variant.
2. Randomly draw a number from 0 to n; if greater than one, append that number of
randomly selected inclusion/exclusion criteria to the definition.
3. Randomly select one task instruction and append to the prompt.
We repeated this process 50 times to produce 50 codebook-guided, human-generated
prompts. Each variant was evaluated on our training dataset, and we identified the prompts
yielding the highest and lowest F1 scores.
These two empirically selected prompts serve two purposes. First, the top-performing
prompt provides a strong baseline against which we evaluate the added value of automatic
prompt engineering, few-shot classification, and additive prompting techniques. The lowest-
performing prompt, by contrast, serves as a test of whether these techniques can ‘fix’ a
prompt which does not, by itself, produce classifications that are aligned with human codes.
Second, the performance gap between these two extremes speaks to the extent to which
reasonable variations in baseline prompt wording can influence model output—and to the
utility of a codebook-guided, empirically informed prompt selection process.
Automatic Prompt Engineering
To automatically generate prompts, we followed an iterative process beginning with a
human-generated baseline prompt (either the bottom or top baseline prompt) as the seed.
At each iteration, we provided this seed prompt within the following meta-instruction:
9

“Generate a variation of the following prompt while keeping the output format.
You may add important information or remove unnecessary information.
Instruction: prompt
Output only the new instruction.”
Using this meta-prompt, we generated five new prompts per iteration. Each was evaluated
on our training dataset, and the prompt yielding the highest F1 score was selected as the new
seed. This process was repeated for five generations, and we selected the highest performing
prompt across all iterations.
Temperature for the classification task was set to 0 while
temperature for the prompt generation was set to 1.
Selecting Examples for Few-Shot Learning
We limit our pool of potential examples from the training dataset to 50 and create 50
random samples of potential few-shot example combinations. For each combination, we first
randomly select a number from 1 to 10; this becomes the number of examples n. Then, we
randomly select n examples from the pool one at a time without replacement. We repeat this
process 50 times to yield 50 distinct few-shot combinations. We evaluate each combination
using the remaining examples in the training set (i.e., those not included in the example
pool) and identify the combination that achieves the highest F1 score for both the top and
bottom baseline prompts.
Additive Techniques
Persona
We generate three potential personas for each construct. For gratitude, we test:
1. You are a language model trained to detect emotions in user text.
2. You are a positive psychologist looking for examples of gratitude.
3. You an expert labeler.
For negative core beliefs and meaning making, we test:
1. You are a caring and brilliant therapist. Your job is to determine if your client demon-
strates that they hold negative core beliefs/is engaging in meaning making.
2. You are a psychology professor. You are looking for examples of negative core be-
liefs/meaning making in writing to show your students.
3. You are a professional psychologist studying negative core beliefs/meaning making in
client writing.
For each construct, we select the persona which generates the highest performance in the
training dataset when prepended to the top and bottom baseline prompts.
Chain-of-Thought
To incorporate chain-of-thought prompting into a zero-shot classification task, we append
the following to the baseline prompts:
“First, explain your reasoning step by step. Then, state your final answer —
either Yes or No — using the format: Final Answer: [Yes or No].”
For few-shot classification, we illustrate this reasoning process by providing chain-of-
thought responses for each of the selected few-shot examples. Because the phrasing of the
reasoning may influence performance, we generate two different reasonings for each example
and evaluate their performance on the training set. For each case, we select the phrasing
that yields the highest F1 score.

Explanations
To incorporate explanations into our prompts, we use the following prompt template:
{Baseline Prompt}
Text: {Example}
Answer: {Answer}
Explanation: Explanation
The number of text–answer–explanation pairs depends on the specific few-shot combi-
nation selected using the procedure described in Selecting Examples for Few-Shot Learn-
ing. Because the content of the explanation may influence performance, we generate two
candidate explanations for each selected example and evaluate them on the training data
(excluding the examples used in the prompt). For each example, we retain the explanation
that yields the highest F1 score.
Models
We perform our experiments using one closed-source, proprietary LLM – GPT-4 from
OpenAI – and one open-source LLM – Llama-3.3. In this article, we are agnostic on the choice
of LLM platform, assessing the utility of prompt engineering approaches for two platforms
and generalizability across platforms. However, there are ethical and privacy considerations
in the choice of LLM provider, which preference the use of open-source and open-access
LLMs when resources allow (Hussain et al. 2024).
Closed-access models, like those from OpenAI, require that data are shared with provider.
At the time of this writing, text provided to OpenAI through the python API are not
retained by OpenAI long-term.
Instead, OpenAI states that they “securely retain API
inputs and outputs for up to 30 days to provide the services and to identify abuse. After
30 days, API inputs and outputs are removed from our systems, unless [OpenAI] are legally
required to retain them” (OpenAI 2025). Still, this privacy policy brings concerns when
it comes to personally identifying information (which, in our case, were removed). On the
other hand, because open-access models can be run locally (ensuring that data never leave
the user’s system), they provide full protections with respect to participant privacy.
We employ GPT models programmatically through the openai Python library and
call Llama through the HuggingFace library. We run Llama within our university’s high
performance computing environment (a necessity because the model is large and stored
locally). In both the GPT and Llama models, we reduce temperature, which determines the
amount of noise included in the determination of the probability of each potential token, to
zero.
Evaluation
To assess the extent to which each technique improves alignment between human and
LLM codes, we report F1 scores with non-parametric bootstrapped standard errors, calcu-
lated as follows: (1) sample n texts and associated human labels and model predictions with
replacement (where n is the number of texts in the development or testing dataset; creating
a bootstrap sample); (2) compute the F1 score for each of 1,000 bootstrap samples; and (3)
calculate the standard deviation of the resulting distribution. Final performance metrics are
accompanied by bootstrapped standard errors and 95% confidence intervals, which reflect
the range of values that would be expected to contain the true metric 95% of the time if
the sampling process were repeated. Narrow intervals indicate greater statistical certainty
in the performance estimate, while wider intervals suggest more uncertainty.

Few-Shot Prompting Can Compensate for Poorly Worded Prompts
and Is Nearly as Influential as Baseline Selection
Tables 3–8 underscore the value of few-shot prompting, particularly when paired with low-
performing baseline prompts. In all six construct–model combinations, the addition of few-

combinations, the bottom baseline paired with few-shot examples performs as well as—or
slightly better than—the top zero-shot baseline prompt.
However, few-shot prompting appears to offer less benefit when the underlying prompt
is already effective.
While the addition of examples often yields small positive changes,
none of the differences between the top zero-shot and top few-shot prompts reach statistical

The specific combination of examples also plays a critical role in determining performance.

Discussion and Recommendations
Across our experiments, our findings reinforce what prior literature has emphasized –
prompting matters for increasing alignment with expert codes (Sahoo et al. 2024; Weber and
Reichardt 2023). While prior work has often focused on general-purpose prompting strate-
gies, our findings point to towards the importance of theory-driven prompting and brute-
force experimentation. Our results suggest that the construct definition, inclusion/exclusion
criteria, task description, and (to a lesser extent) examples provided are more influential
than LLM-specific prompting techniques like personas, chain-of-thought, or explanations.
Zero-shot personas and chain-of-thought only inconsistently improve performance above the
baseline. When examples are added to these techniques (few-shot persona, few-shot chain-
of-thought, and few-shot explanations), performance improves—but rarely exceeds the per-
formance of few-shot examples added to a well-constructed baseline prompt. This is both
good and bad news. On the one hand, chain-of-thought prompting and explanations are
computationally expensive—because they produce longer completions, model run-time in-
creases substantially, as do costs for proprietary models. If these techniques offer limited
additional value, this may provide an opportunity for cost savings. On the other hand, our
findings suggest there are no simple shortcuts to improving the validity of LLM output. If
these results generalize beyond the present cases, they indicate that researchers should prior-
itize testing a wide variety of baseline prompts—human- and/or machine-generated—as this
component has the greatest impact on performance. Given the above results, we recommend
researchers consider the following process for assessing and improving the alignment between
LLM and human construct identification:
1. Generate an initial codebook-guided baseline prompt —including at a minimum a
construct definition and task instruction. Evaluate performance in the training dataset.
If the results are satisfactory, proceed to the final evaluation using a hold-out testing
dataset, reporting performance metrics alongside standard errors and/or confidence
intervals. If improvement is needed, continue to step 2.
2. Generate a diverse set of baseline prompts using components derived from the human
codebook. Variants can be created by combining alternative phrasings of (a) the con-
struct definition, (b) task instructions, and (c) inclusion and exclusion criteria, whether
human-generated, generated through automatic prompt engineering, or both. Evaluate
prompts from this pool by assessing their performance in the training dataset. Select
the best configuration.
3. If resources permit, experiment with few-shot prompting by appending different com-
binations of examples to the best-performing baseline prompt. Evaluate these few-shot
variants in the training dataset and identify the top-performing configuration (whether
16

zero-shot or few-shot). Compare performance between the zero-shot and few-shot ap-
proach either in the training dataset or, if resources allow, a development dataset
(decreasing the likelihood of selecting an approach that was overfit to the training
data).
4. Again, if resources permit, experiment with appending additive techniques to current
best-performing prompt, whether that be the additive techniques discussed in this ar-
ticle (persona, chain-of-thought, and/or explanations), other techniques not discussed,
or new alternative techniques as they arise. Again, compare results, ideally in a devel-
opment dataset.
5. Conduct a final evaluation in a held-out testing dataset, calculating accuracy, precision,
recall, F1 score, and associated confidence intervals to provide an unbiased estimate of
human-machine alignment.
This procedure directs researcher effort toward the aspects of prompt engineering that
our findings suggest have the greatest impact—prompt wording, structure, and example
selection—while emphasizing empirical validation of final outputs.
Limitations
While we believe the above recommendations to be both a reasonable and empirically
driven process, our results, and therefore our conclusions, come with key limitations. First,
our findings regarding persona prompts, chain-of-thought, and explanations are ultimately
null findings. And it is difficult to provide substantive evidence of the absence of an ef-
fect using only a single experiment. In our case, we offer a series of six (admittedly non-
independent, given the same data is used across two or more tests) experiments, increasing
the strength of evidence somewhat. Nonetheless, we cannot rule out the possibility of a Type
II error. Therefore, we don’t conclusively state that persona prompts, chain-of-thought or
explanations do not work, but that, based on the evidence here, they should perhaps be
lower priority prompting techniques for improving LLM performance in the identification of
psychological constructs. Second, our findings come with generalizability challenges: what
works in one scenario may not work in another (Battle and Gollapudi 2024). Again, we
hope that our variety of constructs and diverse sources of data help temper this limitation,
but generalizability is still not guaranteed. Further, model capabilities are certain to change
over time and new prompting techniques are sure to be invented, potentially limiting the
generalizability of our results across model generations. As the nature of LLMs change, how-
ever, our process for prompt generation and evaluation will likely remain relevant. Finally,
we should acknowledge that prompt engineering, as we recommend it, is a time-consuming
process which requires a moderately-sized labelled dataset. Our recommendations only ap-
ply to scenarios where a reasonable number of labelled texts (say 50 to 100) can be set
aside for prompt engineering (not including the labelled texts which should be set aside for
validation). Researchers can and should only embark on this process when resources allow
and when maximizing performance is deemed important. If LLMs will be used to support
or guide clinical decision-making, for example, then this investment will be worth it.
Conclusion
This study demonstrates that prompt engineering, when treated as a systematic and
empirical process, can meaningfully improve the validity of large language model outputs
for text classification tasks in psychology. By programmatically evaluating thousands of
prompt variations across three constructs and multiple datasets, we show that the greatest
performance gains arise not from one-size-fits-all prompting techniques, but from targeted
experimentation with core elements: construct definitions, task framing, and examples. Em-
pirically selecting and validating these components can reduce disagreement between LLM
output and human codes by as much as two-fold. Our findings highlight not only a repli-
cable procedure for improving LLM performance but also the essential role of evaluation as
these models are increasingly applied in high-stakes psychological and behavioral research
contexts.

key_findings.claim: Baseline prompt wording — specifically the construct definition, task framing, and inclusion/exclusion criteria — is the single most influential factor in LLM text classification performance for psychological constructs, outweighing additive techniques such as persona, chain-of-thought, and explanations.
key_findings.quantitative_result: F1 delta between best and worst baseline prompts reached 0.33 for meaning making with Llama 3.3 (F1: 0.33 → 0.66); statistically significant for every construct-model combination.
key_findings.context: Codebook-guided empirical prompt selection across 50 variants evaluated on training data, tested on development set with bootstrapped 95% CIs.

key_findings.claim: Few-shot prompting can effectively compensate for a poorly worded baseline prompt and is nearly as influential as selecting an optimal baseline prompt.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Statistically significant F1 improvements in all 6 construct-model combinations when few-shot examples added to bottom baseline; bottom + few-shot matched or exceeded top zero-shot in 5/6 combinations.
key_findings.context: 50 random few-shot example combinations evaluated in training set; best combination selected; evaluated in development set.

key_findings.claim: Automatic prompt engineering consistently improves poorly worded baseline prompts but provides inconsistent benefit — and can degrade performance — when applied to already well-performing prompts.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Statistically significant improvement over bottom baseline in 5/6 construct-model combinations; one case showed reduction of 0.10 F1 points (meaning making, Llama) when applied to top baseline (non-significant).
key_findings.context: Iterative APE process: 5 generations × 5 variants each, seeded from human baseline, evaluated on training data.

key_findings.claim: Zero-shot persona and chain-of-thought prompting provide only modest, statistically non-significant improvements over baseline prompts for psychological construct identification.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Persona improvements: up to 0.10 F1 gain from bottom baseline but never statistically significant; zero-shot CoT occasionally improved bottom baseline but never significantly.
key_findings.context: Tested across 3 constructs × 2 models = 6 combinations; evaluated in development dataset.

key_findings.claim: Few-shot chain-of-thought and explanation-based prompting yield minimal additional benefit over standard few-shot prompting; performance gains are attributable to the examples rather than the reasoning or explanation structure.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Few-shot CoT and explanations improved bottom baseline in 4/6 combinations, but rarely exceeded performance of standard few-shot; no consistent significant gains over few-shot alone.
key_findings.context: Computationally expensive (longer completions, higher cost for proprietary models) with negligible marginal benefit.

key_findings.claim: The best human-machine alignment is achieved by combining codebook-guided empirical prompt selection with automatic prompt engineering in a few-shot setting using GPT-4.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Final hold-out test performance: Gratitude F1=0.89 CI [0.83–0.95]; Negative Core Beliefs F1=0.70 CI [0.60–0.80]; Meaning Making F1=0.76 CI [0.62–0.90].
key_findings.context: Evaluated in held-out test set (25% of data); represents unbiased final performance estimate.

key_findings.claim: LLM classification performance decreases with increasing construct inference complexity, with performance highest for low-inference emotion recognition (gratitude) and lowest for high-inference psychological constructs (negative core beliefs).
key_findings.quantitative_result: GPT-4 test F1: Gratitude 0.89 > Meaning Making 0.76 > Negative Core Beliefs 0.70; performance gaps most pronounced for Llama 3.3.
key_findings.context: Gratitude classified as low-inference (Cohen's Kappa 0.75), negative core beliefs and meaning making as high-inference (Kappa 0.82 and 0.70 respectively).

key_findings.claim: Few-shot example selection variability substantially affects performance, especially for bottom baseline prompts and high-inference constructs, with some combinations markedly degrading performance.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Histograms of 50 random few-shot combinations showed wide F1 distributions; variation especially pronounced for bottom baseline and high-inference constructs (see Appendix A).
key_findings.context: 50 random few-shot combinations sampled; best combination selected empirically on training data.

key_findings.claim: The best automatically engineered prompt was not produced in the final iteration in 9 of 12 construct-model-baseline combinations, suggesting automatic prompt engineering operates via brute-force exploration rather than iterative improvement.
key_findings.quantitative_result: Best APE prompt appeared in final generation in only 3 of 12 construct-model-baseline combinations.
key_findings.context: 5-generation iterative APE process; best prompt tracked across all generations.

llm_extraction.methods_summary: Empirical evaluation of five prompting strategies (codebook-guided empirical prompt selection, automatic prompt engineering, persona prompting, chain-of-thought, and explanatory prompting) for LLM-based text classification of psychological constructs. Three constructs were studied spanning low-to-high inference complexity: gratitude (N=600, GoEmotions Reddit dataset), negative core beliefs (N=565), and positive meaning making (N=589), the latter two drawn from expressive writing interventions. Two LLMs were tested: GPT-4 (closed-source) and Llama-3.3 (open-source). Data were split 25%/50%/25% into training/development/testing sets at the participant level. Fifty codebook-guided human-generated prompt variants were evaluated empirically; the top- and bottom-performing prompts were selected as seeds for further experimentation. Automatic prompt engineering used 5 generations of 5 variants each. Few-shot examples were selected from 50 random combinations (1–10 examples). Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1, with non-parametric bootstrapped standard errors (1,000 samples) and 95% confidence intervals. Final model performance was evaluated on a held-out test set.
llm_extraction.limitations: 1) Null findings for persona, chain-of-thought, and explanations are difficult to confirm definitively — six non-independent experiments provide moderate but not conclusive evidence against these techniques (Type II error cannot be ruled out). 2) Generalizability is limited: negative core beliefs and meaning making datasets comprised only women, which could interact with technique effectiveness. 3) Potential data leakage for gratitude construct: Reddit GoEmotions data may appear in GPT-4 and Llama training corpora, possibly inflating performance on this construct. 4) Results may not generalize across model generations as LLM capabilities evolve. 5) The procedure requires 50–100 labeled examples for prompt engineering, limiting applicability when labeled data are scarce. 6) Only three psychological constructs tested; generalizability to other domain-specific construct types is uncertain. 7) Experiments are non-independent (same data used across multiple technique comparisons).

relationships.description: Reynolds & McDonell (2021) argued that zero-shot prompting and persona patterns (via 'cultural consciousness') improve LLM performance; this paper extends that work to psychology-specific constructs and finds that persona patterns provide only inconsistent, non-significant improvements.

Brown et al. (2020) established few-shot in-context learning as effective; this paper confirms few-shot prompting substantially improves performance across all construct-model combinations in a domain-specific psychology setting.

Wei et al. (2022) demonstrated strong benefits of few-shot chain-of-thought for reasoning tasks; this paper finds that CoT offers minimal marginal benefit over standard few-shot prompting for text classification of psychological constructs.

Zhou et al. (2022) reported mixed performance for automatic prompt engineering; this paper corroborates that finding — APE consistently improves poorly worded prompts but yields inconsistent results when starting from already strong baselines.

Battle & Gollapudi (2024) found that 'seemingly worthless prompt modifications' can have meaningful performance impacts; this paper supports this through empirical demonstration of large F1 swings across prompt variants.

Lampinen et al. (2022) found explanation prompting improved performance on diverse tasks; this paper extends this to psychology text classification and finds explanations offer minimal additional benefit over standard few-shot examples.

Kojima et al. (2022) showed zero-shot CoT with 'Let's think step by step' substantially improves arithmetic and symbolic reasoning; this paper extends evaluation to text classification of psychological constructs and finds limited benefit in this domain.

methodology_details.approach: Systematic empirical comparison of five prompt engineering strategies (codebook-guided human selection, automatic prompt engineering, persona, chain-of-thought, explanations) in zero-shot and few-shot settings for LLM-based text classification of psychological constructs. Prompts are generated, evaluated on training data, and validated on development and held-out test sets. Bootstrapped confidence intervals are used for statistical comparison.
